REVIEW COMMITTEE

Today’s students grow up in the age where their surroundings are determined primarily by technological connectivity. With the introduction of technology into life, people have gained the chance to get information promptly. The fact that every student and teacher live in the world of screens makes the communication style between them change drastically. Nevertheless, this transition to digital communication has also caused various issues, like cyberbullying, harassment, and even concealed emotional problems.

Digital reporting tools can help schools organize concerns disclosed by students and identify submissions that require attention. StudentShield processes vents and bullying reports submitted through its own forms; it does not monitor private messages, social-media accounts, or all student communications.

To support Saint Vincent Blessed School of Manila (SVBSM), the developers created StudentShield as a reporting and risk-screening platform. It combines a counselor dashboard with automated SMTP email and SMS notification functions. These functions support staff review; their existence does not establish that bullying or psychological harm has been reduced.

The primary goal of StudentShield is to support SVBSM in identifying and responding to emotional distress and reported bullying. Natural language processing screens student-submitted vents, while counselors investigate bullying reports and decide on intervention.

In case there is no central monitoring system present at an educational facility, several issues arise when it comes to tracking student behavior and preventing it before it turns out to be very dangerous. That is why the key elements underlying the development of StudentShield are as follows:
Proactive Risk Detection: Use NLP and local language rules to screen student-submitted vents for signs requiring counselor attention.
Priority Action: Classify vent submissions as Low, Medium, High, or Critical to help counselors prioritize review. Bullying reports follow a separate staff-verification workflow.
Trend Analytics & Monitoring: Leveraging trend data to identify patterns in student wellbeing and empowering the administration with data-driven decision making.
Project Description

StudentShield combines a PHP CodeIgniter 4 web application with a Python FastAPI machine learning service. Students submit vents and incident reports through the web interface, and authorized staff review records through a unified dashboard.

The analysis assigns vents to four risk categories: Low, Medium, High, and Critical. High vents trigger counselor notification attempts; Critical vents also trigger parent notification attempts unless the student selects the parent-hiding safety option. Notification delivery depends on the configured services and connectivity. Bullying reports notify counselors at intake and require staff verification before incident alerts are sent to parents.
The general objective is to design, develop, and evaluate StudentShield as an NLP-assisted emotional-distress screening and bullying-reporting system that supports staff intervention at SVBSM.

To create a Safe Space web platform where SVBSM Junior High School students can submit personal vents and confidential bullying reports, with optional photos or videos as incident evidence. Submissions remain linked to authenticated accounts and are not anonymous to authorized staff.
To implement risk classification using a fine-tuned mDeBERTa model, a GoEmotions classifier, and multilingual rules that assign Low, Medium, High, or Critical screening categories.
To track changes in student risk classifications over a 14-day window using prior risk labels and timestamps stored in the application database.

To integrate SMS and email notifications for counselors and, where the implemented rules permit, parents or guardians, with separate handling for High vents, Critical vents, and verified bullying incidents.

To assess the accuracy of the risk flags through a planned pilot evaluation with SVBSM and examine the system’s privacy controls, including AES-256-CTR storage encryption. Pilot outcomes and formal compliance findings remain to be established.
To develop an integrated online video conferencing module that enables guidance counselors to conduct secure, real-time virtual consultations with students directly within the StudentShield platform.

An authenticated Safe Space and bullying-reporting website for SVBSM Junior High School students, including optional photo or video evidence for bullying reports. Authorized staff can identify the submitting student.
A risk-screening pipeline using mDeBERTa, GoEmotions, and language rules. Its percentages are application screening scores, not clinically validated probabilities of future harm.

A 14-day trajectory function supplied with prior risk labels and timestamps from MySQL. The PHP query selects up to 100 non-archived records in ascending date order. Current trajectory scoring does not depend on a FAISS index.

A unified staff dashboard and configured SMS/email integrations, with counselor-only alerts for High vents, counselor and eligible parent alerts for Critical vents, and staff verification before bullying-incident parent alerts.

Application-level AES-256-CTR encryption for vent text and bullying details in the normal storage path. The current vent controller still has a Base64 fallback if encryption throws an exception; Base64 is encoding, not encryption, so universal encryption-at-rest cannot be claimed.

Registration requires acceptance of displayed terms and privacy information and creates an inactive student account for staff approval. The current system does not store a separate verified guardian identity, signed consent document, or versioned guardian-consent record.

The system includes an online video conferencing feature limited to one-on-one sessions between a student and a designated guidance counselor, conducted within the platform for confidential consultation purposes.
It is not a diagnostic tool for mental illnesses; it is not a prescription for treatment; it is not a replacement for the services of a professional guide counselor.
There is no persistent live-chat or messaging module. One-to-one video consultation is available through Jitsi Meet.
The ML pipelines are configured for CPU inference. Minimum hardware capacity, concurrent-user capacity, and end-to-end latency have not been established by measurements in the official paper.
The project is scoped to SVBSM. Multi-school operation and large-scale concurrent use have not been evaluated in the existing capstone materials.
Internet connection is required at all times to use this service.

The study aims to improve how student concerns are documented and prioritized at SVBSM. The following benefits describe the intended contribution of StudentShield; they are not measured intervention outcomes.

heading: The Client / Organization (Saint Vincent Blessed School of Manila)

section: The Client / Organization (Saint Vincent Blessed School of Manila)
text: The proposed research would provide SVBSM with an up-to-date instrument for dealing with the problem of decentralized report management. Now that the school can count on a centralized procedure, it would be able to avoid unnecessary paper work and verbal notifications of any kind. This will give an opportunity to the administration to better use their guidance staff.

StudentShield gives students a confidential channel to submit vents and bullying reports. Records are linked to their accounts and can be reviewed by authorized staff. For guidance counselors, the dashboard brings together submitted concerns and highlights High and Critical vents for review.

Parents and guardians can receive SMS and email notification attempts for Critical vents and staff-verified bullying incidents involving their children. A student’s parent-hiding option suppresses the Critical-vent parent alert while preserving counselor escalation. Parents are notification recipients and have no login portal.

For the school, StudentShield offers a centralized record of reported concerns, staff actions, and case information. Its access and encryption controls support privacy requirements; a finding of legal compliance cannot be inferred from implementation alone.

One of the key lessons learned during this whole process was dealing with the difficulties of combining various web technologies for developing a system that can link a PHP and CodeIgniter web application with a Python and FastAPI microservice. The team members also learned how to integrate APIs, use AES-256 data encryption, and route notifications in real time.

This project presents a case study on how to implement transformers' capabilities in practical settings. Future research could base their studies on this model, for instance, by improving the NLP engine for different dialects, among other options.

Cyberbullying - Intimidation, harassment, or threat towards a person through electronic communications (Oxford Dictionary, 2020). In StudentShield, it refers to the use of digital means and/or aggression formally reported through the "Bullying Report" Module by SVBSM students.

Data Privacy Act (DPA of 2012 / RA 10173) - Philippine law that protects privacy rights of private and sensitive personal information (National Privacy Commission). It forms the legislative basis of how data is collected, stored, encrypted, and used in the system.

Encryption – A process that transforms readable information into ciphertext to protect confidentiality. StudentShield normally encrypts vent and incident text with AES-256-CTR before MySQL storage; the vent-controller Base64 exception path remains a limitation.

FAISS (Facebook AI Similarity Search) – A library for similarity search over dense vectors. It appears in the earlier StudentShield design but is not used by the current database-backed risk-history function.

Machine Learning – A field concerned with systems that learn patterns from data. StudentShield uses trained language models to screen submitted vent text. Microservice – A separately running service that provides a defined application function. The FastAPI text-analysis service is hosted separately from the CodeIgniter web application.

Natural Language Processing (NLP) - Artificial intelligence subdomain aimed at analyzing, generating, and understanding language in humans (IBM, 2021). In the StudentShield system, it serves to help analyze non-formal student text submissions, which contain a significant amount of slang and informal expressions.

StudentShield – The capstone platform developed for the SVBSM context, combining student-submitted vents, bullying reports, automated screening, staff case management, and eligible SMS/email alerts. No sale or commercial transaction is established by the current paper.

Transformer - Neural network architecture that uses the attention mechanism to establish word-to-word and word-to-sentence connections (Vaswani et al., 2017). In this context, transformers will contribute to improving the understanding of the context of meanings of student vents.
Vent - To let off steam; to vent one's feelings (Merriam-Webster, 2023). The text entry was produced by a student in the "Safe Space" module and aimed at venting their emotions.

Terms of Service (ToS) - Referred to as the legal document describing the responsibilities of the users, system boundaries, information handling procedures, and interaction guidelines for students and administrators using the StudentShield website application.

heading: Improving Large-scale Language Models and Resources for Filipino

section: Improving Large-scale Language Models and Resources for Filipino
text: As Cruz and Cheng (2022) note, transfer learning that uses fine-tuning of pre-trained models on the basis of a language with many available resources (English) and adapts them to the use of the Filipino language, which is resource-poor, is highly useful. According to the results obtained by Cruz and Cheng, multilingual BERT models, which were fine-tuned for the Filipino language, considerably outperformed those trained on a small data set from scratch.

section: Improving Large-scale Language Models and Resources for Filipino
text: The present study discusses the aforementioned hypothesis through the prism of application to StudentShield, where the algorithm operates with texts in Taglish language, which combines English and Filipino languages. It means that the development of a model based only on the Filipino language cannot be considered feasible due to lack of training data.

section: Improving Large-scale Language Models and Resources for Filipino
text: Taking into consideration Cruz and Cheng's experience, the researchers offer to apply the approach of using a pre-trained multilingual transformer (mDeBERTa-v3), which is able to identify language patterns in the sentence, in order to analyze Taglish texts produced by SVBSM students.

heading: 2.3 Synthesis of the Reviewed Literature and Studies

text: StudentShield separates the PHP web application from the Python ML service so they can be hosted and maintained independently. Vent submission still makes a synchronous HTTP request to the ML service; separation alone does not remove inference latency or guarantee uninterrupted submission.

Front-End Student and Administration Portal: The application uses standard HTML5, standard JavaScript, and Tailwind CSS in the frontend. The mentioned above web technologies have been chosen to use because they provide a way to keep the system simple enough to allow fast loading of its pages and navigation by students.

Back-End Application Logic (PHP): CodeIgniter 4 handles routing, sessions, database access, and workflow logic. The current configuration enables the global CSRF filter and role-based access checks. These are implemented controls, not proof that the entire application is free of vulnerabilities.

Database (SQL): MySQL/MariaDB stores user profiles, submissions, incident records, and case data. Sensitive vent text and incident details use CodeIgniter’s AES-256-CTR encrypter in the normal application path, subject to the vent-controller exception noted in the delimitations.

Machine Learning Analysis Engine (Python): FastAPI and PyTorch run the text-analysis pipeline. A separate deterministic function evaluates 14-day risk history supplied from MySQL. The current inference path does not use a FAISS vector store for historical tracking.

Advanced Language Models: The emotion pipeline loads SamLowe/roberta-base-go_emotions. The distress pipeline attempts a local fine-tuned model, then ashlogg/student-shield-mdeberta from the Hugging Face Hub, and falls back to the GoEmotions model if the custom model is unavailable. Training scripts and datasets exist in the repository. The earlier plan to collect 300 counselor-labeled SVBSM entries and augment them to 1,000 samples remains a proposal; the official paper does not document completion of that collection.

Trajectory Tracking: VentController selects risk labels and timestamps from the preceding 14 days and sends them with the current submission. risk_history.py orders these records, appends the current preliminary classification, and computes a trend and recurrence score. The database is the durable history source; the ML service does not retain a per-student FAISS file in the current implementation.

Deployment and Notification: The CodeIgniter web application is hosted on InfinityFree; the FastAPI ML service runs as a Docker Space on Hugging Face. Cloudflare fronts the web domain. SMS gateway and SMTP settings are environment-configured. The PHP production host has no SSH or runtime CLI access.
StudentShield Risk Classification Engine

The current engine combines distress and negative-emotion confidence with equal weights, then applies additive language heuristics and ordered override rules. Historical escalation is evaluated from database-backed risk labels over 14 days. The returned percentage is clamped to the final Low, Medium, High, or Critical band. These screening values are not validated probabilities of a future clinical outcome.

The design separates the web interface and ML engine for independent hosting and maintenance. The web application manages accounts, submission storage, incidents, and staff actions; the Python service supplies screening results. The PHP fallback provides a reduced screening path when the ML result is unavailable.

The original paper adopts an Agile-Iterative development approach so that individual modules can be built and revised as requirements and language-screening rules change. The phases below retain that development plan without treating planned testing or field validation as completed work.

Planning defines the student-welfare problem, the intended SVBSM users, and the core reporting and screening modules. The original paper motivates StudentShield through the need to organize concerns and notify staff; it does not supply a measured baseline of the school’s existing procedures.

The researchers analyzed the needs of the system based on the needs of the users during the process of system analysis. It was necessary to establish the way in which the system would analyze the texts in order to establish possible levels of threats, the way in which counselors will view the reports and the way in which the students will report bullying and venting messages. Database architecture, user privileges, encryption of sensitive information, implementation of machine learning and warning systems were some of the technical needs that were analyzed.

During the system design phase, the StudentShield structure was carefully designed. The researchers developed the database structure, arranged the fundamental components of the system, and determined the relationships between the most essential parts. Also, counselors' and students' user interfaces were created with ease of use and procedure simplicity in mind. As well, the interface between the web application and machine learning service was highlighted, especially with the topic of notification management, risk assessment, and text classification. Process flowcharts, architecture diagrams, and entity-relationship diagrams were one of the design outputs used as deployment tools.
Using the Agile methodology, system development has been carried out in manageable iterations, each iteration on a different feature:
Iteration 1: Fundamental Web Functionalities (Login, Vent Submission, Bullying Reports)
Iteration 2: Integration of Machine Learning (integration of the custom Hugging Face-hosted ML service)
Iteration 3: Security and Alerts (Local SMS Gateway, Audit Logging, and Encryption)

PHP (CodeIgniter 4) and MySQL were used for the backend, while Tailwind CSS and JavaScript were used for the frontend. The Local SMS Gateway for text alerts, SMTP for email OTPs, and ApexCharts for data visualization were added tools.
Based on the system requirements, every important feature will be carefully reviewed. The researchers will make certain that:
Every essential feature, including database storage and one-time password authentication, is verified.
Language screening should be evaluated on labeled examples of slang, Taglish, English, and the supported regional-language expressions; correctness cannot be assumed from the presence of a lexicon.
In emergency scenarios, the automatic local SMS gateway and SMTP alerting function well.

The following step would involve putting the prototype to use in the real world using the production server, environment variables, and API (Local SMS Gateway & SMTP). This would be followed by maintenance process, which will ensure the integrity of both security and functionality of the application. There would be the following events:
Setting up the live database and uploading the CodeIgniter 4 system
Defining the Counselors' and Super Admins' initial roles and permissions
Resolving user concerns or logical mistakes
Modifying the machine learning model to better predict students' language use
Security updates and system backups

Counselors and super administrators sign in with name and password, followed by a six-digit email OTP with five-minute expiry and an attempt limit, unless an accepted remembered-device token applies.
Students log in with name and password only. No OTP is required.
Passwords are stored using bcrypt hashes. The current login flow uses password_verify; the older claim of silently upgrading plaintext passwords is not retained.

The current implementation does not separately verify or retain a signed guardian-consent document. Pending approval must not be described as verified guardian consent.

The original paper proposes keeping records active while a student is enrolled and retaining records for 30 days after graduation or transfer. This is a proposed institutional policy, not an implemented automatic retention workflow.
The proposed 30-day window is intended to allow pending administrative and counseling work to conclude.

Automatic deletion after that window has not been implemented or demonstrated by the supplied paper. The proposed duration should not be represented as a statutory requirement established by this study.
The original proposal also calls for preserving records during temporary inactivity and allowing reactivation on re-enrollment.
Current vent and incident archive operations use soft-deletion fields; these do not by themselves implement an enrollment-based retention policy.
Enrollment-linked archiving, timed deletion, and re-enrollment restoration remain proposed procedures requiring implementation and validation.
Access to retained and archived records shall be limited to authorized school personnel through role-based access controls.
The original paper sets an intended 2–3-second vent-response target, but provides no recorded benchmark. The synchronous ML request and notification calls can increase end-to-end submission time.

The implemented ML request timeout is 60 seconds overall with 15 seconds for connection. A local keyword fallback can supply a screening result after a failed request; no fallback latency benchmark is established.
Dashboard data refreshes via AJAX polling without requiring a full page reload.

The web application is hosted on InfinityFree and the ML service is deployed separately on Hugging Face Spaces. PHP fallback reduces dependence on ML availability, but neither zero downtime nor sub-second response is guaranteed.

Vent and incident text use AES-256-CTR in the normal persistence path. The vent Base64 exception fallback and legacy plaintext-reading compatibility prevent a blanket claim that all stored text is encrypted.
Current password creation uses bcrypt and authentication uses password_verify.
Staff OTP verification uses six digits, a five-minute expiration, and an attempt limit, with remembered-device behavior as described above.
Form submissions are rate-limited (30s for vents, 120s for bully reports) to prevent spam and gateway abuse.
The user management panel is access-controlled to Super Admin only. Counselors are explicitly blocked.
Automatic retention is an unfinished requirement. The current code does not implement automatic end-of-school-year anonymization or the proposed 30-day post-transfer deletion schedule.
The interface is built with Tailwind CSS and is responsive across desktop and mobile devices.
Students can submit a vent in 2 steps: type their entry and click submit.

The study uses an Input-Process-Output (IPO) framework to organize the relationship between student disclosures, application processing, and staff-facing records. Risk scores are automated screening outputs and are not objective diagnoses.
Input actors include Junior High School students, guidance counselors, and super administrators. Parents and guardians are external notification recipients rather than authenticated system users.

System inputs include student vent text, bullying-report details, optional evidence files, user credentials and profiles, parent contact details, meeting requests, and acceptance of registration terms. A separate signed guardian-consent record is not implemented.

Development software comprises CodeIgniter 4 and PHP, Python/FastAPI/PyTorch, the configured mDeBERTa and GoEmotions models, MySQL/MariaDB, JavaScript and Tailwind CSS, SMTP and SMS services, and Jitsi Meet. Hosting is split between InfinityFree and Hugging Face Spaces.
Hardware: Standard computer sets, client web browsers, and active internet connections serving as the physical tools for both system development and end-user testing.

The Process is an overview of the activities involved during the creation, implementation, testing, and continuous improvement of the StudentShield system. This begins with the Planning and Objective Formulation phase, which entails identifying the institutional need for bullying and emotional distress intervention and defining important modules such as the Safe Space Portal, Bullying Report Module, NLP Dashboard, and Alerting System.

The System Analysis phase focuses on gathering and analyzing the requirements of students, counselors, parents, and administrators. During this phase, the researchers determine the system’s risk classification requirements (Low, Medium, High, and Critical), security and privacy requirements, reporting mechanisms, notification workflows, database requirements, and machine learning functionalities.

The System Design phase involves designing the overall structure of StudentShield. This includes the creation of the Entity Relationship Diagram (ERD), Data Flow Diagrams (DFD), software architecture, system flowcharts, user interfaces, database relationships, and the integration design between the web application, machine learning engine, and notification modules.

The development process covers the web interface, Python text-analysis API, SMS/email integration, and application encryption. Formal privacy-policy enforcement and automatic record-retention procedures require separate implementation and validation.

The Testing and Debugging phase involves verifying system functionality, validating predictive model performance, testing notification delivery mechanisms, checking encryption and security controls, and evaluating the accuracy of predictive models in different languages, including Tagalog, English, Bisaya, and Ilocano.

The evaluation plan calls for ISO/IEC 25010-oriented questionnaires and user feedback, followed by statistical analysis. Completed survey ratings and acceptance results are not supplied in the official paper.

Finally, the Maintenance phase ensures the continued reliability and security of the deployed system through production deployment, database and notification service configuration, security updates, backups, bug fixes, machine learning model improvements, and ongoing user support.

Implemented outputs include student submission forms, automated risk labels and scores, staff case views and timelines, eligible SMS/email notification attempts, and one-to-one Jitsi meeting links. Completed evaluation findings and verified reductions in bullying or distress are outside the evidence currently available.

Evaluation of the system will be carried out in the form of feedback from the project itself. It is to be conducted through the analysis of final ratings given by the users and feedback collected from the four types of users, namely Junior High School students (usability aspect); Guidance Counselors (functional suitability and prediction ability); IT Administrators (audit compliance and reliability); and parents (timeliness of alerts).

The retained context diagram describes the existing vent and bullying-reporting boundary at a high level: students submit credentials, vents, and reports; the ML service returns risk and emotion information; staff receive dashboard information and perform verification; parents receive eligible alerts. It is a partial view of these flows and does not depict the meeting module or the risk-history payload.

The system sends current vent text, the student identifier, and prior risk labels and timestamps to the ML service. Parent alerts are conditional: Critical vents respect the parent-hiding option, and bullying incidents require staff verification. High vents are routed to counselors.

Students, counselors, and super administrators use the authenticated functions below. Parents participate as external alert recipients. The earlier use-case figure is omitted because its submission-to-parent extensions do not express the current staff-verification and parent-hiding conditions.
Student: The main user who checks in to report incidents of bullying or create encrypted diary entries.

Counselor: School employees who check vent logs and look into bullying reports after logging in over a secure OTP gateway. When a student is flagged, they are the first to receive emergency emails and SMS alerts.

Super Admin: Uses the shared staff portal and dashboard, manages users and roles, and views audit logs. Counselor-notification lookup targets counselor profiles rather than a separate parent or teacher role.
Parent: A passive actor who gets automated email and SMS alerts when the machine learning classifies their child's vent log as critical risk.
Staff/Admin Login: Name-and-password authentication followed by a six-digit email OTP, with five-minute expiry and a five-attempt limit. Valid remembered-device tokens can bypass a new OTP challenge.
Student Login: Students can log in separately and more easily with just their name and password. OTP is not necessary.

Submit Vent Log: Students write encrypted journal entries. The machine learning risk analyzer, which rates the text and determines a risk level (Low, Medium, High, or Critical), is automatically called for each submission.
Bully Report Submission: Students submit an encrypted incident report on bullying. The counselor office is instantly notified by email and SMS upon submission so they can look into it.
View Counselor Dashboard / Review Vent Logs / Review Bully Reports: Counselor-side features for reading decrypted entries and managing active cases.
View Admin Dashboard / Manage Users & Roles / View System Audit Logs: Admin-side operate for account management and compliance tracking.

Trigger Email/SMS Alert: Notification attempts follow backend rules. High vents notify counselors. Critical vents notify counselors and eligible parents unless parent hiding is selected. Bullying intake notifies counselors; staff verification triggers incident alerts to resolved parent contacts. Rejection blocks those incident-verification alerts, although repeated false-report strikes can separately notify the reporter’s parent.
The distinction between automated screening and staff verification is central to this design: a submitted incident is not treated as proven misconduct merely because it was reported.

heading: 4.3.3 Data Flow Diagram (DFD) or Activity Diagram

section: 4.3.3 Data Flow Diagram (DFD) or Activity Diagram
text: While the Context Diagram presents StudentShield as one system, DFD Level 1 reveals what happens inside the system. The process consists of the following: Manage User Accounts, Analyze Vent Submissions, Process Bullying Reports, Monitor Cases & Analytics, and Dispatch Notifications. Manage User Accounts verifies the user's credentials in the User/Profile Records repository, containing users, students, counselors, and admins. All the significant events related to the management process are recorded in Audit Logs.

section: 4.3.3 Data Flow Diagram (DFD) or Activity Diagram
text: Vent analysis writes its resulting record to vent_logs, while bullying intake writes to bully_reports. Staff review these records through the dashboard and case summary. Notifications use configurable SMS and SMTP integrations; logging is split between database records and a local alerts.json file. The earlier DFD Level 1 is omitted because its direct incident-to-parent path and fixed Gmail/log-storage assumptions do not fully match this workflow.

Super administrators sign in with their name and password through the shared staff portal and complete email OTP verification unless a valid remembered-device token applies. They can review vents and reports, manage users and roles, and inspect audit logs. The older flowchart’s public staff sign-up step is not an implemented workflow.

Counselors use the shared staff login and dashboard. They review vents and incidents, verify or reject reports, maintain case notes and status history, and handle meeting requests. They do not have the super administrator’s user-management privileges. Public counselor sign-up is not implemented.

Students register for approval or use an existing account, then sign in with name and password without OTP. They may submit a vent, select the parent-hiding safety option, file a self or bystander bullying report with optional evidence, and request a counseling meeting. Evidence files are stored in protected application storage and referenced by a database filename. The older student flowchart incorrectly shows student two-factor authentication.

The key in the users table is the main primary key in the database. The `id` attribute in the table is auto-incremented and creates a unique record for all users registered in the system. The `id` can also be seen as the common key that will be used by other associated tables.
users : The primary key `id` in the `users` table is auto-assigned to all registered users

students: In this table, the `user_id` acts as both the primary and the foreign key. Another `id` attribute is not required because there exists a direct mapping between each student profile and their user account.
counselors: This table is similar to the students table with the `user_id` acting as both the primary key and the foreign key linking the counselor's profile to their corresponding user account.
admins: This table also uses the same principle where the `user_id` links the admin's profile to their respective user account.
vent_logs: In this table, the primary key is the `id` because more than one vent log can be submitted by one user. The `user_id` here acts as the foreign key.

bully_reports has id as its primary key. reporter_student_id, victim_student_id, and bully_student_id reference users.id. The schema permits null values; an authenticated intake normally identifies the reporter, while a named victim or alleged bully may remain unresolved.
audit_logs: The primary key of this table is `id`. There is a foreign key in this table as well, and that is `user_id`.
sms_logs and email_logs: Both of these tables have `id` as their primary key. In these tables, `student_id` refers to `users.id`.

In conclusion, the tables of profile data of students, counselors, and admin have `user_id` as the primary and foreign key of `users` as well as one-to-one relationships. But in the case of logs and reports tables, they have their respective primary keys and foreign keys as well.
This section documents the testing process to be followed, guided by the design specifications and functional requirements listed above.

For assessing the efficiency, usability, and technology performance of StudentShield, an established process for gathering and analyzing data will be employed. The method for analysis is that of a mixed-method, wherein the researcher employs both qualitative and quantitative measures. Analysis of quantitative data gathered through evaluation of users will be accomplished through descriptive statistics. Additionally, in order to outline the methodology for measuring the effectiveness of the model during the next phase of implementation of the system, standard text classification measures are listed to assess the machine learning model's efficiency in future operation.

For an efficient evaluation of the StudentShield prototype, the following data collection techniques will be used by the researchers in assessing the design and usability of the prototype. The first approach that will be applied is the Questionnaire/Survey. This will require the utilization of ISO 25010 quality criteria when assessing the functionality, reliability, usability, and efficiency of the prototype. The second approach that will be applied is the Interview. The qualitative information will be gathered through this approach concerning the alerting functionalities of the prototype for the school staff members. The third approach that will be employed is the Observation. The usability of the mockup of the dashboard and the report form will be evaluated using this method by means of guided testing. Finally, the Document review approach will be adopted in order to determine whether the data fields and workflow of the prototype match those of the school guidance counseling manuals and paper forms.

The intended study site is Saint Vincent Blessed School of Manila (SVBSM), at 732 Instruccion St., Sampaloc, Manila, 1000 Metro Manila, as identified in the original paper. The target setting is the Junior High School and its guidance and IT staff. Completed field evaluation at that site is not established by the supplied evaluation materials.
The main subjects of the study in the prototype evaluation phase are categorized into three different user groups. These include all of the following groups involved in making the StudentShield work:

The Student Body: These would be the main users of the software that would use the "Vent" module and the incident reporting tool. The involvement of these users in the testing phase of the prototype would be essential to measure the usability, navigation, and security of the interaction with the system.

Guidance Counselors and Responders: These user categories will receive notifications for all incidents and will respond accordingly. Their participation in prototype evaluation is important for testing the administrative dashboard’s functionality and ease of navigation.

IT and System Administrators: These users are responsible for technical support operations on the platform. Their participation in prototype evaluation is important for assessing the system architecture, user experience flow, and compliance with data privacy requirements.

Non-probability sampling will be used in sampling respondents for prototype testing, namely purposive sampling. Purposive sampling is appropriate in the given case due to the fact that the project is in the prototype phase of development and the main goal of the research will be the receipt of quality feedback from potential users.

Purposive sampling will allow selecting those respondents who will correspond to the target characteristics of end-users. In particular, among the selected respondents, there should be guidance counselors that will work with the dashboard, technical security specialists, and some representatives from the student council who represent students.
Questionnaire data, when collected, will be analyzed using the following descriptive statistics to describe average ratings and variation among respondents.
Frequency counts and percentages break down the demographic profile of the participants.
The formula for the percentage is as follows:
Formula: P = (f / n) × 100
Where:
P = percentage
f = frequency
n = total number of respondents

The weighted mean is computed to determine the measure of central tendency of each criterion. The weighted mean provides an estimate of how the system is rated by users. The formula for the weighted mean is as follows:
Formula: WM = (Σfx) / n
Where:
f = frequency
x = assigned weight of each scale point (1 to 5)
n = total number of respondents

The mean describes the average rating, while standard deviation describes variation in the ratings. A lower standard deviation indicates more closely grouped responses; a higher value indicates greater dispersion.
The formula for the standard deviation is as follows:
Formula: SD = √[ Σf(x - x̄)² / n ]
Where:
f = frequency of each rating

The planned classifier evaluation will use accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score against labeled test examples. These metrics describe classification performance; they do not establish diagnostic reliability.
Accuracy = (TP + TN) / Total
Precision = TP / (TP + FP)
Recall = TP / (TP + FN)
F1-Score = 2 × (Precision × Recall) / (Precision + Recall)

TP stands for true positive, TN stands for true negative, FP stands for false positive, and FN stands for false negative. These metrics will be used to examine the accuracy of the model in identifying potential threats in students' writing.

The implementation separates the PHP web application, the Python ML service, and external communication services. This division supports independent deployment; it does not establish measured availability or response-time results.

The CodeIgniter application is hosted on InfinityFree with MySQL and the public studentshield.app domain behind Cloudflare. GitHub Actions uploads web-app-ci4 through FTP. The production PHP host has no SSH or runtime CLI, so database upgrades require reviewed phpMyAdmin steps. A future hosting migration would require configuration and compatibility checks.

The FastAPI/PyTorch service is packaged for Hugging Face Spaces using Docker. The configured API default points to ashlogg-student-shield-official.hf.space. Repository deployment automation uploads ML files through the Hugging Face Hub tooling; it does not deploy through Azure VM container cleanup or SFTP. The checked-in workflow names an underscore-form Space target, so synchronization with the configured endpoint requires deployment verification. SMTP and the configured SMS gateway supply notification delivery attempts.
